blocks.text: Interference and diffraction of light provide evidence for its wave nature, while the photoelectric effect and the Compton effect prove its particle nature. Similarly, the experiments of Davisson and Germer and of G. P. Thomson show the wave-like nature of electrons, while J. J. Thomson's experiment to find e/m required the particle-like nature of the electron. In the same way we are forced to assume both wave-like and particle-like properties for all matter (electrons, protons, neutrons, molecules) and for light, X-rays and gamma rays. Matter and radiation have a dual 'wave-particle' nature; this is called wave-particle duality.

Niels Bohr's principle of complementarity states that both the wave and the particle aspects are needed for a complete description of radiation and matter. Both are always present and either may be revealed by an experiment, but not both at once in a single experiment. Which aspect appears depends on the experiment: a diffraction grating in the path of a light beam reveals it as a wave, while light hitting a metal surface must be treated as a stream of particles. Light behaves as a stream of photons when it interacts with matter and as a wave while travelling from a source to where it is detected. In effect, all micro-particles propagate as if they were waves and exchange energy as if they were particles.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: If electrons behaved only as particles with no wave properties, a beam sent at a double slit would pass through one slit or the other and make two bright images of the slits on a screen. In reality the screen shows a pattern of bright and dark fringes, as with light: the electron waves from the two slits interfere.

blocks.alt: Two panels. (a) A beam of electrons is aimed at a double slit; behind it the screen shows only two bright images of the double slit. (b) The same beam and double slit; the screen shows a pattern of bright and dark fringes.
blocks.caption: Do you know?: a beam of electrons and a double slit, (a) if electrons behaved as discrete particles, (b) in reality (original drawing after the textbook's Do you know? box).
